Coverings: sets of cells

Source: vignettes/coverings.Rmd
coverings.Rmd
library(a5R)
library(sf)

A covering is a set of A5 cells at one resolution that stands for an area: the cells of a polygon, of a disk around a cell, or of a cap of a given radius. An a5_covering vector holds one covering per element, so coverings sit in a data frame column next to the features they describe.

What a covering stores

A covering is stored compacted: every complete group of four sibling cells is replaced by their parent, and a trailing compaction marker records the resolution the stored cells stand for.

raleigh <- a5_lonlat_to_cell(-78.64, 35.78, resolution = 11)
cap <- a5_spherical_cap(raleigh, radius = 12000)
cap
#> <a5_covering[1]>
#> [1] res 11: 57 cells (24 stored)

The stored cells are parents in the A5 index, whose outlines do not nest: drawn directly they overlap their neighbours and leave gaps. Everything that combines, tests or measures coverings works on the stored cells without expanding them, which keeps it fast for coverings that stand for millions of cells. To draw a covering or join it to data keyed by cell, expand it with a5_uncompact(), as the figures here do. Where it helps, a second row shows what the same covering stores.

Building coverings

a5_polygon_to_cells() returns one covering per feature. By default a cell belongs when its centre lies inside the polygon; containment = "overlapping" also takes every cell the boundary touches, so the cells cover the polygon without gaps.

nc <- st_read(system.file("shape/nc.shp", package = "sf"), quiet = TRUE)
nc <- st_transform(nc, 4326) # A5 works in WGS 84 longitude and latitude
alleghany <- nc[nc$NAME == "Alleghany", ]

centre <- a5_polygon_to_cells(alleghany, resolution = 11)
overlapping <- a5_polygon_to_cells(alleghany, resolution = 11, containment = "overlapping")
c(centre, overlapping)
#> <a5_covering[2]>
#> [1] res 11: 77 cells (44 stored)  res 11: 102 cells (42 stored)

The functions that start from a cell return one covering per centre cell: a5_grid_disk() takes every cell within k steps, a5_spherical_cap() every cell whose centre is within a distance, and a5_cell_to_subcell() the finer cells whose centres lie inside a coarser cell.

disk <- a5_grid_disk(raleigh, k = 3)
cap <- a5_spherical_cap(raleigh, radius = 8000)
coarse <- a5_cell_to_parent(raleigh, resolution = 9)
subcells <- a5_cell_to_subcell(coarse, resolution = 11)

a5_compact() turns any set of cells into a covering, and as_a5_covering() builds coverings from cell lists or from the stored form written by other A5 libraries.

Measuring coverings

a5_count() gives the number of cells a covering stands for, and a5_area() its area. A5 cells are equal-area, so the area is the count times the area of one cell. At resolution 11, where a cell covers about 8 km², it tracks each county’s true area closely:

nc$cells <- a5_polygon_to_cells(nc, resolution = 11)
nc$cell_area <- a5_area(nc$cells, units = "km^2")
head(nc[c("NAME", "cells", "cell_area")], 3)
#> Simple feature collection with 3 features and 3 fields
#> Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON
#> Dimension:     XY
#> Bounding box:  xmin: -81.74091 ymin: 36.23397 xmax: -80.4351 ymax: 36.58973
#> Geodetic CRS:  WGS 84
#>        NAME                         cells        cell_area
#> 1      Ashe res 11: 139 cells (55 stored) 1126.9112 [km^2]
#> 2 Alleghany  res 11: 77 cells (44 stored)  624.2602 [km^2]
#> 3     Surry res 11: 176 cells (62 stored) 1426.8804 [km^2]
#>                         geometry
#> 1 MULTIPOLYGON (((-81.47258 3...
#> 2 MULTIPOLYGON (((-81.23971 3...
#> 3 MULTIPOLYGON (((-80.45614 3...

Each point is a county; the dashed line marks equal areas. The covering area is within 1% of the county’s for the median county and about 6% at worst, because each cell straddling a county boundary is in or out by its centre. Finer resolutions reduce the error.

Combining coverings

a5_union(), a5_intersect() and a5_difference() combine coverings without expanding them.

a <- a5_spherical_cap(a5_lonlat_to_cell(-78.72, 35.78, 11), radius = 10000)
b <- a5_spherical_cap(a5_lonlat_to_cell(-78.58, 35.78, 11), radius = 10000)
a5_union(a, b)
#> <a5_covering[1]>
#> [1] res 11: 62 cells (26 stored)
a5_intersect(a, b)
#> <a5_covering[1]>
#> [1] res 11: 16 cells (10 stored)
a5_difference(a, b)
#> <a5_covering[1]>
#> [1] res 11: 23 cells (17 stored)

The result of each operation is compacted again, so a covering that comes out of a union stores its merged interior as coarser cells.

They work element by element, recycling a length-one argument, so one call intersects every county with a single cap. With one argument, a5_union() merges every covering in a vector into one.

near_raleigh <- a5_spherical_cap(raleigh, radius = 60000)
nc$share_near <- a5_count(a5_intersect(nc$cells, near_raleigh)) / a5_count(nc$cells)

state <- a5_union(nc$cells)
state
#> <a5_covering[1]>
#> [1] res 11: 15,672 cells (1,356 stored)

Both coverings in each pair must be at the same resolution, or it is an error. A5 cells do not nest across resolutions: a resolution-11 cell can straddle the edge between two resolution-10 cells, so a set of cells at one resolution does not translate into a set at another.

a5_union(state, a5_spherical_cap(a5_cell_to_parent(raleigh), radius = 60000))
#> Error in `a5_union()`:
#> ! union failed for element 1: Cannot combine cells at resolution 11 with
#>   cells at resolution 10

Testing coverings

a5_contains() tests cells against a covering. Indexing points at the covering’s resolution turns it into a point-in-polygon test, decided cell by cell: a point counts as inside when its cell belongs to the covering.

set.seed(1)
lon <- stats::runif(300, -81.4, -80.9)
lat <- stats::runif(300, 36.35, 36.6)
points <- a5_lonlat_to_cell(lon, lat, resolution = 11)
inside <- a5_contains(centre, points)
table(inside)
#> inside
#> FALSE  TRUE 
#>   150   150

Near the county line the answer follows the cells, not the line: a point just outside it is inside when its cell’s centre is in the county, and the reverse.

a5_overlaps() tests whether two coverings share any cell. With centre containment every cell belongs to the one county holding its centre, so neighbouring counties never overlap. With containment = "overlapping", cells along a shared border belong to both:

pair <- nc[nc$NAME %in% c("Alleghany", "Ashe"), ]
by_centre <- a5_polygon_to_cells(pair, resolution = 11)
gap_free <- a5_polygon_to_cells(pair, resolution = 11, containment = "overlapping")
a5_overlaps(by_centre[1], by_centre[2])
#> [1] FALSE
a5_overlaps(gap_free[1], gap_free[2])
#> [1] TRUE

Shared cells are in aqua.

Drawing and joining

a5_uncompact() expands coverings to their cells. simplify = FALSE keeps one element per covering, ready for tidyr::unnest():

per_county <- a5_uncompact(nc$cells[1:3], simplify = FALSE)
lengths(per_county)
#> [1] 139  77 176

Uncompacting can build a great many cells: a covering of France at resolution 18 stands for about a billion. a5_uncompact() refuses to build more than .Machine$integer.max cells; work with the covering itself where possible.

Storing coverings

Coverings keep their compaction marker in storage, as in the other A5 libraries. a5_covering_to_arrow() writes them to an Arrow list<uint64> column that DuckDB, Python and JavaScript read with the resolution intact, and a5_covering_from_arrow() reads them back, normalising coverings written elsewhere. See vignette("arrow-parquet"). a5_is_valid() checks that a covering built by hand is well formed.
